notes.title: Murder Is Game Over Series Retrospective – Part 1
notes.content:
[img]https://clan.akamai.steamstatic.com/images/6138946/92d01e216e79e6660b894f6601cd3cc2b3ee871e.png[/img]

After developing and releasing 3 “Murder Is Game Over” titles in 2 years, I’ve had some time to pause and reflect on what I like most about each one. These are my thoughts on the series as a whole.

Best exploration – Murder Is Game Over

My initial concept for this game was to have a murder mystery that emphasized exploration much more inspired by RPGs than adventure games. In hindsight, the world design from the first game was well done in terms of giving the player freedom to move around the world at their choosing. The map shape is based on a series of interconnecting circles including the castle's ground floor, connecting the second floor and the sealed wing, and finally, a secret passage connecting the castle to the surrounding countryside. The method of murder also relies heavily on the way the map makes a seemingly inaccessible area easy to reach through a clever shortcut. Not only is the exploration mechanic effective for the player, but it also serves as part of the storytelling and narrative.
[img]https://clan.akamai.steamstatic.com/images/6138946/7f80e1fc4e2a5ded79aded636f18e96e6a8fc179.jpg[/img]

Which game in the series has my favorite villain? Find out in part 2 coming next!

I'm creating the fourth game in the series. Please wishlist it (link below). Thank you for your support!
Matt

notes.title: ⚙️ New game mechanic in Murder Is Game Over: Deal Killer 🕵️‍♂️
notes.content:
[img]https://clan.akamai.steamstatic.com/images/6138946/f71305e0bbe3dec1e1167ae3ca37bed63cee3161.png[/img]

❄️🏔️ With Murder Is Game Over: Streaming Death I wanted to introduce the idea of being chased around by a “ghost” like in Scooby-Doo. In the second half of that game, Elias Abel (actually the killer in disguise) randomly appears while exploring and moves toward the player. The easy difficulty mode is very straightforward. The hard difficulty mode also randomizes the time before the ghost appears so that it’s much more unexpected. The world map is designed to provide lots of opportunities for being chased, and lots of space to maneuver around an aggressive ghost.

[img]https://clan.akamai.steamstatic.com/images/6138946/62d5658c8707f1a3c64a2b2448238df54f425b36.png[/img]

With Murder Is Game Over: Deal Killer instead of going big, the concept was to go small spaces. I wanted the player to get the feeling of claustrophobia and being stuck in a small hotel with nowhere to go. There’s little room for a ghostly crook to hide or sneak around. So this concept got me thinking about what other mechanics I could use for a hero or villain to trick people.

That’s how I came up with the new costume mechanic for this new game in the series. Just because there’s no space to hide doesn’t mean there aren’t other ways that a person can be deceptive. Partway through the game, our detectives discover a trove of costumes that Guy can wear as a disguise. The disguises will prompt instances of mistaken identity and different (sometimes extremely silly) reactions from suspects. The costume theme might also play an essential part in how the crime was committed, and how the detective solves the case. 

[img]https://clan.akamai.steamstatic.com/images/6138946/c0bbc39daa2f9f9c6e11d1e3089836e51eac9dbc.png[/img]

Do you prefer being chased around a village by a spooky ghost, or being stuck in a mountain top chalet during a blizzard with nowhere to go? As the Murder Is Game Over series continues to evolve, my goal is to come up with different gameplay concepts and mechanics that make each title feel different and unique. 🥸

Thanks for reading!

Matt (indiedev of Murder Is Game Over series) 

https://store.steampowered.com/app/2478850/Murder_Is_Game_Over_Deal_Killer/

notes.content:
[img]https://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/6138946/b7be70889b5cab375671414d5fcaa4a5f54822ce.gif[/img]

Indie game publisher Meridian4 is proud to announce the upcoming release of [b]Jumphobia: Homeward Bound[/b], a side-scroller platformer created by indie developer Wix Games. Scheduled for official release in Q1 2022, [b]Jumphobia: Homeward Bound[/b] is a fast-paced platformer with no jump button!

[img]https://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/6138946/61d7c7cb0ede4e0f0ab9a1c7322974d3452c5bc8.png[/img]

[b]Jumphobia: Homeward Bound[/b] is a game built around the premise of getting from "A" to "B" by jumping - but not when you want to! All Jump-bots are built with a failsafe to limit their maneuverability, meaning that you as the player can only automatically jump when you reach the edge of a drop or platform. That's right - it's a platforming game without a jump button!

[img]https://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/6138946/3c2b38efa1d16cb2479e571a473657742ce69ae5.png[/img]

Artist statement: The concept for the original Jumphobia game was to try and see if a platform could still be fun without a jump button. It’s the most important element to almost every platformer - so what would happen if it isn’t there? The result was a game where you have to think about everything differently. The difficulty no longer comes from pressing jump at the right time in order to clear the gap, it’s now a question of which gap is the right one to clear - or how can I make it past this obstacle without the freedom to jump whenever I want? The original game was built for a large variety of platforms including the web, so simple graphics and small file size were a necessity. With this new game, we want to really up the quality and push the concept to its limits, with a much higher level count, new lighting systems and 3D graphics, and a fully-fledged story with 3D cutscenes. I started making games as a 13-year-old working from my bedroom, a year later I released my first popular web game Duck Life and created Wix Games the year after in 2010. Since then we’ve had a number of hits and grown to a full-time team of 3.

[img]https://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/6138946/e564a9feb5d089721515e0181e31d1be1f7a5380.png[/img]

notes.title: Meridian4 News - Hirilun Developer Blog
notes.content:
[img]https://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/6138946/d92ea1604cef0fa892fc6c8c935c675559b2a988.gif[/img]

Welcome! Today we want to talk about how we have selected the art style of Hirilun. We want to make a kind of dark style, with a comic feel. So we decided to use an outline for everything, that way we have the feel of a comic, and also is very clear to see a limit of an element. Very useful on a first-person platformer.

And to emphasize the important aspects of the game, like collectibles. We make it all black and white, and it makes the feel dark and useful also to see what is important to the game and attract the attention of the player.

[img]https://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/6138946/5a868b3463c89013687d8930d77486eb065bcc62.png[/img]

Plaza was the first level we made, and it has changed a lot over time. At first, it was much simpler, and it was designed with the idea that it needed to be easy to keep playing even if you fell. We also wanted different paths so you could choose if you preferred to take the upper way through windows and roofs, or the lower one through benches and terraces.

The most remarkable changes were visual: Plaza became a more polished and imposing level, and it now gives the feeling of a dark city. You can feel it just by looking at it.

[img]https://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/6138946/e2c51085851d2398e3d40d8c5b706752e00cf087.png[/img]

When we start to think about what skills we will add, we had one thing in mind: we wanted that the skills have some synergy together. The main idea behind the skills was to open new paths using them, so you had to think and see if a path is possible or not.

The most powerful skill is the dash, that skill opens up a lot of paths, but, when is combined with sprint and glide it becomes even more powerful.

We thought also about other skills like using a rope, walking on the wall, or reversing the time skill. But after all, we decided to keep it simple, and in the end, we think that we have made a good decision.

Thank you all for your support!
Gone Mad Studios

notes.title: Meridian4 News - Paladin Dream Black Friday / Holiday Season Game Update
notes.content:
[img]https://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/6138946/3e421082f02e384b8866abfb6791154835d79fae.gif[/img]

It’s been really enjoyable and inspirational to watch players stream Paladin Dream. It feels like playing God and watching people explore the world I created, and I also get to see which parts are celebrated, and where the game could be better or less confusing. I’ve gotten lots of positive feedback about the story, and I wanted to focus this update on showing more information about the world.

[img]https://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/6138946/68383540a8f4929bdc3e0e8b334b9fa0d5874187.jpg[/img]

The demon worshiping cult is malicious, reclusive, and possesses black magic to keep outsiders away. I wanted to show the extent to which they’ve gone to protect their temple (which was crudely dug out of a city wall). In the update, Josiah explores an MC Escher-like looping room and a hallucination that projects his fear. This dungeon is intended to be full of creepy traps. The fortune-teller in Nazarfang encounter is also expanded a bit, to give the player some early insight into the 3 different religions and how they interact.

[img]https://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/6138946/ee311ab4446d59c7fb1787b30db4574ce13d5b02.png[/img]

The northern wilderness is an area that is mostly not settled, and wild animals have free reign. Organized religion does not have much influence here. I created a new encounter where Josiah spars with another adventurer and their wild animal companion. There’s also a new battle with Josiah’s Reflection (think Link’s Shadow in Zelda games) that requires a bit of logic to win. To ease a side quest that involves a decent amount of backtracking, and I added a way for Josiah to jump down the mountain with a certain item. Making it to the top of Starcross Peak requires Josiah to leave civilization behind and examine his beliefs from a different perspective.

I fixed some minor bugs including dialog, art, and game balance. When you reach a new level, there is also a new common event that fires to tell the player to check and see if they’ve learned a new spell. Hopefully, this will lead to players realizing there are multiple ways to manage their resources. It’s great to get feedback and continue expanding the game.

Hope everyone has a wonderful holiday season and thanks for supporting Paladin Dream!

Matthew

notes.title: Paladin Dream update - Temple of the Wilds
notes.content:
Paladin Dream is excited about offering FREE new content for the game at the end of August. The update includes a pagan / nature-themed dungeon with new enemies, items, a mini-game, and a bit of story. It also features new achievements and new music.

Several publishers I spoke with mentioned that they focus on post-release content updates as part of their publishing strategy. Since Paladin Dream has been gradually expanding from a minimum viable product, I’ve been generally comfortable with this idea. As a creator, I frequently think about what else would be fun to add to the game world, what stories could be told, and how to communicate the game’s themes more clearly.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40226109/cd4957ad342019d8f89d95e0029be9f04a2eb3da.gif[/img]

One of the main ideas in Paladin Dream is the interaction between religions. The story mostly focuses on the conflict between the paladin religion and the demon religion, but there is also a third religion, which is the nature religion. The nature religion is presented as neutral, but generally not explored much in the game. So this update allows the player to enter a nature / pagan theme dungeon concentrating on this religion with expanded content.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40226109/648b5ab14e751446b2223387c713879d485aa3dc.gif[/img]

The nature religion is generally ancient and a bit secretive, so the entrance to this dungeon is a little difficult to locate. You’ll need to have found a certain symbol of this religion, and then there is a new area with a book that details the whereabouts of the temple. Once you obtain this item and find a certain landmark on a map, you’ll be able to go inside the Temple of the Wilds.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40226109/3cc442c63be6240a4f923555ded6f40a1f1f1dd3.gif[/img]

One path inside the temple takes you to an optional boss battle. You might find that certain weapons or spells are not effective against this enemy, and have to figure out what type of attack will deal damage. (Hint: The paladin and demon religions don’t like each other, the nature religion is neutral.) When you win, you’ll unlock a unique armor, and learn more about the spirits of the old world.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40226109/5a98d133ef1b4d7555fe9db8f38f59a3e7c68f76.gif[/img]

Also in this dungeon is a meadow where you’ll have to catch a frantic, fast-moving fairy. It’s not easy, but with a bit of patience and luck, a new item to boost your magic stats will be your reward. Don’t forget to read the inscription on the statue to learn more about another character you’ve met earlier.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40226109/aeaabd137d524bfc410be2c1a6a8d1c9c413d20a.gif[/img]

Lastly, there is a store specializing in new nature / pagan goods with some worthwhile and useful items only available here. Wanted to remove a curse during battle? Here is your chance. Pick up some new supplies before continuing the adventure.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40226109/75e751ba5882c4d22f24737c6f6724fad4ceb77e.gif[/img]

Thanks for supporting the game, and have fun exploring the all-new Temple of the Wilds!

notes.title: The Writing of Paladin Dream
notes.content:
Paladin Dream was inspired by a short story I wrote in high school, which you can access in the link below. [i](Don’t worry, there are no game spoilers!) [/i]
https://hitheryongames.s3.amazonaws.com/promotion/Dream.pdf

This was done for the King Arthur unit in English class and contains many characters from Aurthurian lore. Adrielian Abbey is loosely based on Camelot, for example. But the unique ideas I imagined in my short story formed the foundation for Paladin Dream, with many similar plot points and concepts. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40226109/6c2173cb076a194017c43af2135abc91a94e17d1.jpg[/img]

[b]Dream Duel[/b]
Both stories begin with a knight that loses a duel in a recurring dream. The lookalike enemy is the same. The mountain cave far away is the same. The identity of the rival duelist is different. Getting permission from the authority figure is the same. 
[b]
Rival Duel[/b]
In King Arthur, Sir Kay is sort of a bullying oaf, and in my story he loses his temper and falls off a drawbridge. In Paladin Dream, Sir Kroy is less physically tough but more spiteful and malicious. Since Josiah is generally regarded as a sturdy and athletic knight, it made more sense to give him a rival who would try to bully him physiologically rather than physically. In both cases, the hero takes care of business and leaves their home.

[b]Religious Bandits[/b]
Both stories have the plot point of bandits who continually sack a town because of their loyalty to religion. This idea is also similar to The Seven Samurai / The Magnificent Seven where a poor village employs mercenaries to defend them against a threat. In the original story, the bandit leader mistakes the hero for a villager, whereas in the game the interaction makes it clear that the paladin is recognized but underestimated.
[b]
A Witch’s Forest[/b]
Both stories have the element of a witch enchanting a forest so that the hero is unable to pass through until gaining a magic item. The gas mask in my older story is likely inspired by post-apocalyptic RPG Crystalis, and is a bit of a weird anachronism in context of Arthurian lore. The Fairy Flower is a better choice. Dierdre the Witch is less of a villain than Morgana. She’s more of a pagan / Celtic witch (not the Halloween and broomstick kind) and proves to be a bit crazy. 

[b]Enemy City[/b]
Each story has a part where the hero must pass through an enemy city and avoid guards who would otherwise attack them. In the original story, Balyn has a magical cloak, and in Paladin Dream, it’s possible but unnecessary to obtain this item. In Paladin Dream, the role of the rival city is greatly expanded where we learn that there’s a nefarious scheme being hatched there. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40226109/da3e27babb2baa81d768b1a10a3620a0ca68384b.jpg[/img]

[b]Return Home[/b]
Both stories have an element where the hero returns home to discover something they didn’t know before. In the original story, the knights ride home across the land, but in Paladin Dream the method of return is different. From a gameplay perspective, it didn’t make much sense to have the player backtrack across a huge map, so the plot created a solution to this logistical problem.

[b]Writing Help[/b]
I want to extend a huge, public thank you to my friend Geoffrey Golden, who consulted with me on smoothing out the plot difficulties I was having early on. He is the one person I could not have made this game without since otherwise, I’d still be struggling to form a coherent plot instead of being a game developer. I don’t remember many of my early erroneous ideas, but at one point the hero character was a monk, I wasn’t sure whether or not to have a final boss battle, and there was an extraneous character who was murdered but had no other reason to exist.

I worked really hard on the story for Paladin Dream, and I hope the effort shows through. The short story is one of a small number of creative writing samples that I’m actually proud of, and it was a challenge to adapt a 10-page story into a more complex RPG. Play the game and let me know what you think!

Please wishlist the game! Thank you all for your ongoing support of this project! I really appreciate it. 🙏

notes.title: Game Design Influences for Paladin Dream
notes.content:
Prior to working on Paladin Dream, I had worked on many visual novels, dating sims, and a few RPGs and rhythm games. I knew that romance in games wasn't something I found terribly interesting as a player, and I don't have time to play (or develop) a ridiculously long RPG like Square-Enix or Bethesda titles. My goal was to be short and polished rather than long and rough (or unfinished), and to focus on story, exploration, and combat (in that order of priorities). So here are some of my influences.

[b]Dragon Warrior 4[/b]
Dragon Warrior 4 is structured with 4 smaller quests before the big main quest, with each being like a small self-contained game. The small quests are quite enjoyable, and the player characters feel unique rather than being a blank slate. Since I was initially concerned with scope, my goal was to make Paladin Dream comparable to the 4 small quests in Dragon Quest 4. I also wanted to give Josiah a distinct identity and personality. Not everybody is going to like everything about Josiah, but he has a strong sense of self and doesn't try to be everything to everyone. I wanted to do something as focused as Ragnar, Alena, Taloon, or Mara and Nara where the quest makes sense in the context of the character. 
[previewyoutube=gHtnOxKhCtU;full][/previewyoutube]

[b]Bioshock[/b]
Being around Boston when Bioshock was popular, Ken Levine was a big influence on my design philosophy. I wanted to avoid cut scenes because they get in the way of gameplay. The dream sequence could have been a cut scene but instead, it's a playable area. Another pointer Levine used to talk about was keeping the plot easy to follow. He cited the example that in Indiana Jones: Raiders Of The Lost Ark if you pause the movie at any time and ask what Harrison Ford is doing, he's looking for the ark. Likewise, in Paladin Dream, if you stop the game at any moment and ask what Josiah is doing, he's trying to discover the meaning of his dream. Also like Bioshock (which takes place in Rapture), Paladin Dream focuses on a small countryside region rather than across a whole planet map. 
[previewyoutube=AffpO05p4V8;full][/previewyoutube]

[b]
Tunnels & Trolls: Crusaders Of Khazan[/b]
A relatively obscure PC game from my childhood, T&T was difficult, visually unspectacular, and deeply amazing. The world felt real because each area was filled with detailed encounters, and there were no training wheels so it was possible to get annihilated by a powerful monster even early on. Some might criticize this, but for me, it told the truth because in the real world if you're not careful and make bad choices you'll get your butt kicked too. The visuals were plain and at times barely functional, but the rich descriptions and dialog text more than made up for it. Sometimes graphics in your imagination can produce a more marvelous image than even the coolest and most detailed sprite. Some encounters modeled after these principles were the traps in the city and temple, as well as rich dialogs with the witch and the final boss. 
[previewyoutube=UdyweTwSo2s;full][/previewyoutube]

[b]Visual Novels[/b]
As I mentioned, prior to Paladin Dream I had worked on many VN devteams. Just because romance routes aren't my thing doesn't mean I don't enjoy anything about the genre. Dialog choices are enjoyable. Characters that feel alive rather than merely being signposts for information are critical to storytelling. One mechanic that's original to Paladin Dream (as far as I know) is the battle encounter within a book. Paladin Dream has several places where you read a book within the game, and while reading the book you're exposed to a battle as part of the book storytelling. In one case the fight is trivial and in another it provides some challenge. I wasn't comfortable writing 100,000 words in a VN, but being somewhat close to 10,000 words of the dialog was fine with me. I wanted the player to feel like they're in a believable world region, and not just focus on looking pretty.

[b]Other Games and RPGmaker[/b]
I don't want to just list all my favorite games, but I do want to shout out to the brilliant (albeit divisive) Super Columbine Massacre RPG! Controversial subject matter aside, this game taught me that RPGmaker can be a compelling platform for many kinds of content, including something like a documentary film. Paladin Dream isn't meant to be shocking, but had I not experienced SCMRPG! I may not have been as inspired to use RPGmaker as a storytelling platform. If RPGs are a metaphor for life then RPGmaker is a powerful tool to focus on storytelling without struggling with the technical difficulties of programming. It was great to be able to cut right to the core experience without having to reinvent the wheel of building gameplay systems from scratch. If I were to develop another game with the same creative values I would consider using RPGmaker again for this reason.

Please wishlist the game! Thank you all for your ongoing support of this project! I really appreciate it. 🙏
https://store.steampowered.com/app/1592120/Paladin_Dream/

All the best,
Matthew
HitherYon Games

notes.title: The Music of Paladin Dream
notes.content:
Before being a game developer, I've been a professional music composer for many years. I've also been a lifelong fan of RPG music, idolizing composers like Nobuo Uematsu and Koichi Sugiyama and being inspired by singers like Jennifer Stigile. Technically I worked on my first RPG soundtrack music as a high school sophomore, back in a time that would be dating myself. As a professional, I ended up working on many visual novels and dating sims, and an anime band I created became popular. But I never worked on as many RPGs as I wanted to, and never had the opportunity to do a complete RPG soundtrack. So this was (eventually) an opportunity for me to reach that goal.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40226109/9fb19c4203468e79f95c3e62dbc5e84e5830b85f.gif[/img]

The first piece I wrote for Paladin Dream was a vocal song called "Adriel's Hymn." Prior to Paladin Dream I was in demand writing vocal theme songs, and won an award for "Seasons Of The Wolf" from a game review website. However 2020 was also a difficult year for me involving an unusual amount of  reliability issues with singers on important client projects. Because of this, I first arranged "Adriel's Hymn" using Vocaloid software in lieu of a real singer. Fortunately I had a positive relationship with a singer named Mioune, and I decided to offer her the opportunity to sing.  While she lives in France, she also speaks English very well with a strong British accent which was a wonderful aesthetic choice for a game inspired by Arthurian lore. Suffice to say, Mioune's performance breathed tremendous medieval fantasy credibility compared to the robotic Vocaloid version. (Had she passed on the project, I probably would have kept the Vocaloid version because I was so frustrated with singers in general!)

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40226109/a356c3b8fdd82e2b6e348faf66bd3e545720fccc.jpg[/img]

[url=https://leetmusic.bandcamp.com/track/adriels-hymn]Adriel's Hymn - Mioune Vocals[/url]

[url=https://hearthis.at/cdmqjgpm/adrieloid-.5/]Adriel's Hymn - Vocaloid Demo[/url]

A significant number of the tunes in Paladin Dream are songs that I first conceived in high school and college for friends who were aspiring game developers. Obviously I have more advanced skills and better production tools than were available in those days, but the melody and chords are the same. I also changed some ideas from my original arrangements to better fit the tone of the world of this game. Generally I wanted the player to feel relaxed while exploring a dream-like world with religious themes, accented by music box and choral singing elements. After doing client work for 10+ years, it was refreshing to know exactly what I wanted and do exactly what I wanted. I find myself to be more effective when I am able to play the game, compared to when a client tells me to copy a piece from some other game. In this case I didn't have to spend time trying to figure out how somebody else thinks. 

[url=https://hearthis.at/cdmqjgpm/oldmusic/]Old RPG Music[/url]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40226109/b8a707bc469185f5f9ff09a9879284bae2b9857d.png[/img]

[url=https://leetmusic.bandcamp.com/track/majestic-building]Paladin Dream - Majestic Building[/url]

[url=https://leetmusic.bandcamp.com/track/starcross-mountain-range]Paladin Dream - Starcross Mountain Range[/url]

Every cool RPG has an epic final boss battle theme, so I created a secondary arrangement of "Adriel's Hymn" to sound more lively and intense. Additionally, Mioune recorded vocals on an evil demon cult ritual worship hymn with made-up words. Later when expanding the scope of the game, I would love to create more vocal music and I'm still thinking about the approach. I'm not sure if it's appropriate to have a longer anime-like theme song for a story like this, or whether it might be fitting to create another religious hymn. Or both? It's always energizing to get feedback from players in terms of making further creative decisions.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40226109/ea29f5d61352cd1d2b6adf8bb6be48f66912aafb.png[/img]

[url=https://leetmusic.bandcamp.com/track/nazarah-kadai-rahm]"Nazarah Kadai Rahm" - Demonic Ritual Hymn[/url]

Currently Paladin Dream has 23 original music tracks totaling nearly 30 minutes of music. I hope that the players enjoy the music I created as a labor of love, and of course the soundtrack will also be available as DLC.

All the best,
Matthew
HitherYon Games

notes.title: The World Design of Paladin Dream
notes.content:
In 2019 I went on a trip to Italy with my family. I was born in Milan and lived my first year and a half there, but I had not been back since then and I have no conscious memory of it. So it was a personally powerful experience for me, as well as the joy of being surrounded by stunning architecture from the ancient world. Our travel plans lasted 18 days, and I was fortunate to experience numerous cities and regions of Italy. Since Paladin Dream is inspired by medieval Europe, I also imagined the world modeled after places in Italy that I had visited.

[b]Cathedrals[/b]

With The Vatican as the center of Catholicism, Italy has many beautiful churches and cathedrals. We toured the rooftop of the famous Duomo di Milan, as well as visited other religious buildings in different cities. While churches had similarities, they each had their own unique character. The Duomo had rooftop stairwells reminiscent of the iconic level leading up to the battle with Dracula in Castlevania. A more somber church in Naples had a memorable crypt below the sanctuary. Florence and Sienna had more brightly colored churches. I wanted to capture the sense of history and respect I felt being in these areas, which led to some creative choices constructing Adrielian Abbey.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40226109/22cde5bbb3b1f754769f5f4941e98650ef01ca5f.jpg[/img]


[b]Tuscany[/b]

Tuscany is a region with lots of rolling hills, farms, and home to the incredible hilltop city of Sienna. While driving through Tuscany we stopped to tour a small castle town that felt right out of Dragon Quest. The warm, lush scenery of Tuscany inspired the land surrounding the abbey, and I wanted to share the sense of tranquility and peace I experienced in this part of the journey.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40226109/0de76d62ca0eef2da85128a2baa3898df8fc54d1.jpg[/img]

[b]
Bologna, Florence, and Naples[/b]

These three cities are all very diverse, but elements of each inspired design choices with Nazarfang and the surrounding area. Bologna used to be surrounded by a wall, and parts of it still stand today. The walls of Bologna inspired the walls of Nazarfang, which are heavily fortified and divide the city into different districts. Florence is a more artistic city, which still gives the impression of the Italian renaissance period. The Greatway District in Nazarfang draws influences from Florence, with its affluent hotels and shops, and elegant streets. Naples today is worse off sociology-economically than northern Italy, and the streets are less safe. (At one point in Naples a man on the street asked my aging father if he wanted to buy illegal drugs.) Naples also has underground tunnels, as well as an impressive fortress we visited, and these sights inspired the Underbelly District, Palace District, sewers, and catacombs.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40226109/693b775962b415c1a59f0ea21f38b203cf74fa92.jpg[/img]

[b]Gressoney / The Alps[/b]

Gressoney is a sparsely populated village high up in the Italian alps mountain range. Staying overnight in a mountain lodge in Gressoney overlooking the town was extremely relaxing. The region is home to small farms, as well as enormous mountains that are too rugged for civilization. I even observed little adventurer-constructed paths up the steep cliffs that looked barely safe enough to walk on. Gressoney inspired the village of Duskmont, and the mountain wilderness above.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40226109/6a0619cdf88da6feedb1e07b923d3e16b63b4ce7.jpg[/img]

[b]
Pompei and Herculanium[/b]

Visualizing the Dream[/b]

Originally my design for Paladin Dream was to have 3 main regions in the game, including the area around Adrielian Abbey, the area around Nazarfang, and the mountain waste. Compared to being in Texas with its modern buildings, enormous superhighways, and broad plain, Italy felt like a very compact area with tight spaces. To make the exploration feel more European I kept the same feeling of close quarters when exploring the cities and countryside. With Italy’s gargoyle statues and religious themed paintings with devils, my real-life travel experiences helped to transform my vision and create an aesthetic where a story about a paladin felt natural and believable.
